subtype: Approach: revising the plan after treatment response [Revision]
passage:
It was exam week for the children, the monsoon had cut the road twice, and Madhav's father was tired and sick to his stomach after the first round of treatment. The plan on paper was not working.
On Tuesday Madhav and his wife Leela sat with the doctor. "We can adjust the timing and the plan," the doctor said. "Tell me what you're seeing at home." Leela had it written in a small diary.
That evening they redid the week. Madhav asked his manager to start later on treatment days. Leela swapped the school run with a neighbour. They also trimmed two spending items to cover the change.
Papa was quieter at supper, but ate more than he had in days.

qa.q: Who did Madhav and Leela meet on Tuesday?
What was Madhav probably feeling when he saw the first treatment plan was not working?
qa.a: Madhav was likely worried and guilty as he watched his father suffer, which is why he was quick to sit with the doctor.

qa.q: What could the family do if the second plan also causes problems?
qa.a: They could go back to the doctor with the diary notes and adjust again, rather than waiting or guessing at home.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt keeping the diary and reorganising the week?
qa.a: Leela probably felt stretched but purposeful, since the diary gave the doctor clear detail and made a hard week manageable.

grounding: The passage shows a family who, after side effects, talk to the doctor about changes, rework schedules at work and home, and adjust spending.

subtype: Approach: revising the plan after treatment response [Revision]
passage:
The first month of Rukmini's treatment went exactly as the family had planned on paper. Then the side effects arrived: nausea after every session, and a tiredness that kept her in bed for two days at a time. The plan her daughter Simran had drawn up, with Rukmini taking the bus alone to Thursday sessions and Simran working normal hours at the Pune office, stopped working.
Simran didn't try to push through. She wrote down every side effect and when it happened, and at the next appointment asked the doctor whether anything could change. The doctor adjusted the timing of the sessions and added medicine for the nausea.
Then Simran rewrote the rest. She asked her manager to let her work from home on Thursdays and Fridays. She booked a cab for session days instead of the bus. She moved money meant for a holiday into the treatment fund. Rukmini, lying on the sofa, said, "You changed everything." Simran said, "The plan had to change. You didn't."

qa.a: The timing of the sessions, and added medicine for the nausea.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when the first plan stopped working?
qa.a: Simran was likely worried and stretched, but chose to adapt calmly rather than push through.
Recording side effects for the doctor first, then adjusting work, travel and money to fit the new reality.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel when she says "You changed everything"?
qa.a: Rukmini likely feels grateful but a little guilty about the disruption, which Simran gently eases.

grounding: It shows a family responding to side effects by talking to the doctor about changes and then updating work, home schedules and money instead of clinging to the first plan.

"Didi, Papa threw up again after the session. That's three weeks in a row."
"I know. And he's too tired to go to the shop even on good days now," Parul said. "Our plan assumed he'd feel normal between sessions."
"So what do we do? Just push through?"
"No. We tell Dr Iyer everything on Monday. I've written down each side effect and the day it happened."
"And if the doctor changes the schedule?"
"Then we change ours. You said your college lets you take Wednesday mornings off?"
"Yes, I asked."
"Good. I'll ask my boss about working from home on session days. And we stop pretending Papa can run the shop. We'll ask Rakesh Uncle to cover two afternoons."
"What about money? The shop's income will drop."
"We'll use what we'd set aside for Diwali. And the hospital's social worker said she'd go through options with us."
Anjali let out a breath. "Okay. New plan."

qa.q: What has Parul written down for Dr Iyer?
qa.a: Each side effect and the day it happened.

qa.q: How does Anjali feel at the end?
qa.a: Anjali feels relieved, letting out a breath once there is a new plan.

qa.q: What makes their revised plan realistic?
qa.a: It starts with the doctor's view, then adjusts college, work, the shop and money to how Papa actually feels.

qa.q: How might Papa be affected by the new plan?
qa.a: Papa no longer has to push himself to the shop and has family with him on session days, which may ease his tiredness and worry.

grounding: It shows sisters responding to their father's side effects by taking notes to the doctor and reworking schedules, the shop and money rather than sticking to the first plan.
